# FortID CTF 2026

> Every fortress has a weakness. Find your way in.

## When is it?

FortID CTF begins on Friday, 9 October 2026 at 20:00 CEST / 18:00 UTC and runs for 48 hours, ending on Sunday, 11 October 2026 at 20:00 CEST / 18:00 UTC.

The CTF is over.

Registration is open now. Register your team before the competition begins.

## What is it?

A capture-the-flag competition is a competitive hacking event: think IOI or ICPC, but for cybersecurity. Teams work through challenges involving cryptography, reverse engineering, binary exploitation, web vulnerabilities, digital forensics, open-source intelligence, and the occasional idea that refuses to fit neatly into a category.

Every challenge has a concrete objective. Reaching it reveals a secret string called a flag, such as `FortID{some-secret-value-here}`. Submit the flag to earn points. When time runs out, the team with the most points wins.

Success rewards curiosity, careful experimentation, and a deep understanding of how computer systems behave when pushed beyond their intended limits. Some challenges are approachable first steps; others are built to keep experienced players busy.

FortID CTF is organized by the TBTL team in Zagreb to bring together people who enjoy cybersecurity, hard technical problems, and learning by breaking things thoughtfully.

## Competition format

This is a jeopardy-style CTF: challenges are independent, grouped by category, and worth points when solved. Expect challenges from:

  * Intro — Friendly first steps and warm-ups for the platform.
  * Web — Finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in web applications.
  * Crypto — Breaking incorrect uses of cryptography and insecure protocols.
  * Rev — Understanding what compiled software does without its source code.
  * Pwn — Exploiting vulnerable programs running on remote systems.
  * OSINT — Finding and connecting information from public sources.
  * Misc — Forensics, esoteric systems, unusual formats, and everything else.

## Rules and fair play

  1. Flags use the format `FortID{...}` unless a challenge explicitly says otherwise. Do not attempt to brute-force flags.
  2. Compete as one team. A participant may belong to only one team and may collaborate only with their own teammates during the event. There is no limit on the size of a team.
  3. Generative AI is forbidden. Do not use LLM chatbots, coding copilots, autonomous agents, or locally hosted generative models to analyze challenges, produce solution code or payloads, or provide solution guidance. Normal documentation, search, debuggers, decompilers, symbolic solvers, and scripts written by your team remain allowed.
  4. Keep challenge knowledge within your team. Sharing or requesting flags, hints, partial solutions, payloads, or writeups while the CTF is running is strictly prohibited.
  5. Stay within challenge scope. Do not attack the platform, scoreboard, landing page, organizers, other teams, or unrelated systems. Avoid denial-of-service, broad scanning, brute force, and high-volume automation unless a challenge explicitly requires it.
  6. Submit flags as you solve. Deliberate flag hoarding or dumping a batch of flags near the end is not allowed.
  7. Keep the event welcoming. Be respectful, communicate in English in shared event spaces, avoid spam, and keep usernames, avatars, and messages free of offensive or NSFW content.
  8. Cheating disqualifies the whole team. When organizers verify a fair-play violation, the entire team will be removed from the competition. Organizers may ask a team to explain a solve or provide supporting work, and decisions on competition integrity are final.

When in doubt about a tool, target, or technique, ask before using it.

## Questions and announcements

Join the FortID CTF Discord for announcements, questions, challenge clarifications, support, and event status updates.

## Prizes

### 🏆 Competition winners

There are no prizes for placement on the competition scoreboard this year, apart from eternal glory and street cred on CTFtime.

### ✍️ Best writeup prizes

We will award at least five prizes for the best writeups, with each prize worth at least €50. Depending on the number and quality of the writeups we receive, we may award additional prizes and/or increase the value of individual prizes.

Everyone is eligible, regardless of their final ranking. To qualify, the writeup must be publicly available on the internet—for example, as a blog post, public repository, or YouTube video.

Have fun, be inventive, and leave the infrastructure standing.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Summary of how the exploit works

#  | Stage  | Mechanism
--- | --- | ---
1  | Leak the ELF base  | `%41$p` prints `ask_oracle`'s saved return address, which is always `elf_base + 0x1664`. Slot 41 is `rbp+0x08`, past the buffer, the canary and the saved `rbp`.
2  | Locate the target  | `blessing` is at `elf_base + 0x404c` per `nm` - a writable `unsigned int` in .bss, so Full RELRO, NX and the canary are all irrelevant.
3  | Put the target address into an argument slot  | `question[256]` sits at `rbp-0x110`, which equals `rsp` at the `printf` call, so the buffer is printf's first stack argument (slot 6). Padding the format string to 16 bytes places `p64(blessing)` in slot 8. It has to go last, because the address contains null bytes.
4  | Drive the character counter to 0x1337  | `%4919c` emits 4919 characters, and 4919 == 0x1337. The field width counts the printed character itself.
5  | Write  | `%8$hn` takes slot 8 as a pointer and stores the counter there as two bytes. The upper half of the `unsigned int` is still zero from .bss, so `blessing == 0x1337` exactly.
6  | Collect  | Menu option 2 passes the comparison in `receive_blessing()`, which calls `win()` - and that simply prints `flag.txt`.

# FortID CTF-26: Sticker Booth Pwn Writeup

Posted Oct 13, 2026

By Yusuf Tas

FortID CTF-26: Sticker Booth Pwn Writeup

Contents

FortID CTF-26: Sticker Booth Pwn Writeup

Today I have another unnecessarily long pwn writeup for you: `Sticker Booth` pwn challenge from FortID CTF 2026. It features my favourite pwn challenge approach: easy and short solution but getting there requires understanding the code deeply. No shell, no libc involved. Keep reading to see what is this challenge about, but be aware this is going to be a long ride…

## First Look

Initial checksec reveals it is statically linked, No PIE binary. We are provided a documentation and available commands in the binary, which indicates it is a heap menu type of challenge. Though upon inspecting the decompiled code, heap is not really used but a custom memory manager `xalloc` is implemented to handle memory operations by using a preallocated 16kb pool memory. Honestly, it took me quite a long time to go over each commands, what they do etc. I believe it is necessary to understand the binary first before we can solve the challenge, so I decided to make you suffer the same pain I suffered during the CTF: going over each command in the binary :) But seriously, it is going to be a long writeup, I know because I am writing this part after I finished everything :) If you are already aware of how the commands work, which structures they use, how memory is allocated etc. feel free to skip to OOB Write to see the actual bug and how I solved this challenge,

## Decompilation (Fetish)

During the CTF, I realized I have a new fetish: making ghidra’s decompilation output as readable as possible. This challenge involves multiple structures and a custom heap manager. When such stuff is involved, ghidra decompilation looks menacing. Offsets are everywhere, weird numbers and conversions. It makes reading the decompiled code output a PITA. I started investigating critical structures used in the code: `Item, Photo, Sticker, Block` and figured out what each field does based on the usage in the code and defined them in Ghidra to make decompiled code reading much easier to deal with. Maybe I spent a bit too much time on this that I didn’t have enough time to solve this during the CTF… Here is a summary of these structures and how they look like in structure viewer in Ghidra:
    
    // 40 bytes total
    struct Item {
        char     name[24];
        uint32_t type;
        uint32_t _pad;
        void    *data;
    }
    
    struct Sticker {
        uint16_t refs;
        uint8_t  type;
        uint8_t  trusted;
        uint32_t len;
        uint64_t ticket;
        char     body[];
    }
    
    // Header 16 bytes then pixels array
    struct Photo {
        uint32_t w, h, stride;
        uint32_t _pad;
        uint8_t  pixels[];           // r g b a
    }
    
    // 0x18 bytes
    struct Block {
        uint64_t offset;
        uint64_t size;
        uint32_t in_use;
        uint32_t extra;
    };

In summary we have `items that hold different types: photo, sticker, custom. Items hold a pointer to memory in pool region. Size and shape of that memory depends on which type of item it is. Blocks are used by xalloc like a arena manager to handle where the allocated blocks are in the pool region`
